title: Braid on trousers, aprons and the Labor Day Parade route
summary: Reel 2 begins with uniform braid, then Barbarin describes the Labor Day Parade and its route.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Paul Barberin, March 27, 1957, reel 2. Was there any braid on the trousers or was it just on the colors? No, it was on the side. On the side, like a tuxedo. Yeah, I like a tuxedo, that's right. It was really nice.
Did the band ever wear aprons like the mumboe did?
No, no. No, I've never wore that, no. I don't know, like the Masonics and anything? No, no, no. In the old days who wore aprons?
What kind of aprons did they have? Did the Masonics or the others? The Masonic and our art fellas and Michael O'Groen Schumer and those people like that. What dance?

Oh no, on Labor Day, Labor Day Parade. Labor Day Parade was a parade. That was another nice parade. They'd have all the bands out. All the bands. They were bands they could get. They could see a parade. And those things were never coming back no more. Where would the parade start and end up? Or like the Labor Day Parade? Well, Labor Day Parade, well, I'll tell you as far as I know about it, Labor Day Parade would start at the River Canal, right on that part. And they'd come down, come around Cloud Street. I mean, down in Ramport to Espinade. Espinade, I guess they would take, go back up on the other side of Ramport, come up a piece and they'd go maybe to, you know, it's that domain or, you know, one of those streets in Cutting. We'd come back around Claymore like that. And I think most of the time they would end up at the Poise Burns Hall in those days down there on Ferris Street. It was a long parade, though. Wear bands, colored bands, too. Yeah, white women colored bands.
